teaser: He gave up copying other painters, moved to the mountains, and painted a cliff that swallows people.
review_notes:
Fan Kuan's remark about learning from nature rather than from men is reported in the Song imperial catalogue (Xuanhe huapu); wording here is a paraphrase.
Signature discovered in 1958 by Li Lin-ts'an of the National Palace Museum, in the foliage at lower right; it is not legible in this image so no spot points to it.
Dimensions 206.3 x 103.3 cm.
Title inscription at top right attributed to Dong Qichang (1555-1636).
Museum display restriction (short showings, long rests) stated in general terms; check current policy wording.
'Fan Kuan' as a nickname meaning broad/generous; given name Zhongzheng.

lesson.text: Fan Kuan began the way most painters did a thousand years ago: by copying. He studied the landscapes of an admired older master, Li Cheng, and worked hard to paint like him. Then he decided it had been the wrong road. Old accounts have him concluding that it was better to learn from things themselves than from another man.

So he left. He went to live among the peaks of northern China, where, the same accounts say, he would sit all day looking at rock, or walk out on snowy moonlit nights to stare. He was a Daoist, part of a tradition that sees nature as the great teacher, and he was in no hurry.

This hanging scroll is what that looking produced, around the year 1000. It is ink with faint color on silk, and it is tall: over 2 meters (nearly 7 feet). Stand in front of it and the cliff begins above your head. How did he organize so much stone?
The picture is stacked in three layers, each one farther from you.

lines.label: Near
lines.text: A row of boulders along the bottom edge. They are the size of houses, yet they take up barely a tenth of the scroll. This is where you are standing.

lines.label: Middle
lines.text: Two wooded hills with a stream cutting between them. Trees, a path, buildings: the scale of human life. It fills about a quarter of the height.

lines.label: Far
lines.text: The mountain. One blunt mass, pushed right up to the front and given nearly two thirds of the silk. Nothing softens it or sets it back.

lesson.text: Chinese painters call this kind of picture monumental landscape: the mountain is the main character, and everything human is measured against it.

Measured is the word. A cliff only looks huge if something small stands beside it. Fan Kuan knew this, and he slipped his measuring stick into the lower right, almost the same brown as the ground it walks on.
The “travelers” of the title are somewhere in this picture, with their animals. Can you spot them?

spots.title: The mule train
spots.text: A line of pack mules steps out from under the trees, heading left along the bank, with drivers walking beside them. Each animal is a few millimeters long. Now look up again at the cliff.

lesson.text: That is the shock the painter built: the eye finds the mules, jumps back to the peak, and the mountain grows. The men are not heroes or pilgrims. They are hauling goods and do not look up. Nature here is not hostile. It is simply on another scale.

For centuries nobody could find a signature on the scroll. In 1958 a researcher at the National Palace Museum finally spotted the two characters of Fan Kuan's name, tucked among the leaves behind the mule train.

Up close, the cliff face is not painted in broad washes. It is built from thousands of short, pecking dabs of the brush, laid over one another until the silk looks weathered. Later painters named them “raindrop strokes.” They are why this rock seems to have weight and grit rather than just an outline.
But a wall of stone that reached all the way down would feel like a backdrop. Fan Kuan needed air between the layers, and he made it without painting anything at all.

lesson.title: Where the layers meet
lesson.text: Three places where the mountain and the valley touch.

spots.title: The mist
spots.text: A pale band of almost bare silk hides the foot of the mountain. Because you cannot see where the cliff lands, it seems to hover, and the distance behind the hills feels enormous.

spots.title: The waterfall
spots.text: A thread of unpainted silk drops down a dark cleft and vanishes into the mist. It is the only thing moving on the cliff, and the only bright vertical.

spots.title: Rooftops
spots.text: Temple roofs rise among the treetops on the right-hand hill. People have settled here, quietly, just under the cloud line.

spots.title: The stream
spots.text: The water that fell from the cliff reappears here, tumbling over rocks between the two hills. You can almost hear what the waterfall is too far away to give you.

lesson.text: Follow that water and you have the route of the whole painting: down the cliff, through the fog, between the hills, past the mules, out toward you. The picture is still, but it has a current running through it.
“Fan Kuan” was a nickname. His given name was Zhongzheng, but people called him Kuan, meaning “broad” or “easygoing,” because of his generous, unbothered character. The nickname is the one he signed.

The big black characters in the top right corner are not his. They were written some six hundred years later by Dong Qichang, a painter and powerful critic, who labeled the work as Fan Kuan's. His opinion carried so much weight that the label has stayed on the mount ever since.

The scroll belonged to China's emperors for generations. In the late 1940s, during the civil war, it was crated with the best of the palace collection and shipped to Taiwan, where it is now among the most treasured objects in the National Palace Museum.
You cannot count on seeing it. Thousand-year-old silk and ink fade under light, so the museum brings the scroll out only for short showings and then rests it in storage for years.
A man who quit imitating others ended up as the one everybody imitated. For Chinese landscape painters, this cliff became the measure of what a mountain should feel like.

Which leaves a question worth carrying to any landscape, painted or real. When you face something this large, are you the viewer standing safely outside it, or one of the small figures on the path, too busy to look up?

quiz.question: What did Fan Kuan decide after years of copying an older master?
options: That he should copy several masters instead
That it was better to learn from nature itself
That landscape was not worth painting
quiz.explanation: He left to live in the mountains and study them directly.

quiz.question: Why are the mules and drivers painted so small?
options: To give the mountain its scale
Because the silk was damaged there
Because they were added by a later owner
quiz.explanation: Tiny figures are the measuring stick that makes the cliff feel immense.

quiz.question: What separates the great cliff from the hills in front of it?
options: A band of mist made of nearly bare silk
quiz.explanation: The pale mist hides the mountain's base and creates depth.

quiz.question: What are “raindrop strokes”?
options: Drips of ink left by accident
Short dabs of the brush that build up the rock's texture
Lines used to paint the waterfall
quiz.explanation: Thousands of small pecking marks give the cliff its weathered surface.

quiz.question: Where was Fan Kuan's signature finally found in 1958?
options: Hidden in the leaves near the mule train
On the back of the scroll
In the large writing at the top right
quiz.explanation: It was tucked into the foliage at the lower right; the writing at the top is Dong Qichang's.

quiz.question: How much of the scroll does the mountain take up?
quiz.explanation: The far layer dominates, with the foreground boulders given only a sliver.

facts.text: The waterfall is painted with thick white pigment.
facts.explanation: It is a thread of unpainted silk left between dark ink.

facts.text: The scroll is more than 2 meters tall.
facts.explanation: It stands over 2 meters, nearly 7 feet, so the cliff rises above the viewer.

facts.text: The National Palace Museum keeps the scroll on permanent display.
facts.explanation: It is shown only briefly and then rested for years to protect the silk and ink.
